title: Proxyless egress + control plane segmentation: notes and proposed pattern
content:
Purpose and scope:

This is a working note exploring an alternative to heavy sidecar meshes for egress+ingress routing across regions. The goals are: reduce per-pod compute overhead, improve tail-latency for latency-sensitive inference paths, simplify cross-region failover, and keep strong mutual-TLS identity (mTLS) guarantees. Scope: platform-engineering decisions impacting control plane segmentation, egress selection, identity/cert rotation, and operational test plans. Not covering per-model kernel selection or runtime batching logic in depth.

Background / motivation:
- Our existing service mesh experiments (Envoy sidecar) provide rich routing features and mTLS but add CPU/GPU host contention during high-throughput LLM workloads, and complicate cold-starts for inference processes.
- We need deterministic egress behavior for three tenant classes: latency-critical (real-time inference), throughput-batch (offline embeddings), and admin/control (telemetry, config).
- Multi-region presence means routes can prefer local region endpoints but must gracefully fail to remote regions or to fallback model variants.

Design goals and constraints:
- Strong identity: workload-to-workload authentication using short-lived certs (SPIFFE/SPIRE or equivalent).
- Minimal per-pod overhead: avoid full sidecar where possible; allow a proxyless mode that leverages kernel-level facilities or light runtime hooks.
- Deterministic routing: per-tenant policy configurable via control plane (can pin tenant to region/model variant).
- Observability: per-route latency/cost metrics and trace continuity across proxyless handoffs.
- Safety: safe fallback policy when control plane is unreachable or certificate authority is partitioned.

Proposed pattern (high level):
1) Control plane segmentation: region-local control planes with global coordination layer
   - Each region runs a control plane instance responsible for local routing policies, certificate minting (short-lived leaf certs), and telemetry aggregation.
   - A lightweight global coordinator holds global policies (quota, org-level pinning) and pushes deltas to region control planes via a signed replication stream.
   - Reasoning: regional CP reduces cross-region control latency and isolates a region failure; global coordinator enables consistent enterprise-wide policies and audits.

2) Proxyless mTLS at the runtime boundary
   - Workloads link against a small library (or use platform runtime integration) that performs: SPIFFE identity fetch, TLS handshake with kernel TLS (or user-space TLS optimized path), and selective connection instrumentation for tracing.
   - This library exposes a simple socket wrapper so apps can keep native sockets but get cert-based identity and automatic rotation.
   - For environments that must have a sidecar (legacy apps, special routing), we continue to support Envoy/sidecar mode.

3) Egress selection and weighted path scoring
   - Routing decision factors: configured route policy (pinned region/model), measured p50/p95 latency to candidates, estimated per-token cost (based on batch size and hardware), and recent error-rate spike signals.
   - Score = w1*(policy_score) + w2*(latency_norm) + w3*(cost_norm) + w4*(availability_penalty). Weights are tunable per-tenant class.
   - Default behavior: latency-critical tenants prioritize policy_score and latency_norm; batch workloads prioritize cost_norm.

4) Fallback semantics and graceful degradation
   - Local region unavailable => try preferred remote region(s) with same model family and compatible quantization profile.
   - If only higher-latency cheaper variants exist, prefer them only if tenant policy allows cost-tradeoffs; otherwise fail fast with clear error codes.
   - Control plane unreachable: clients fallback to last-known routing table (cached signed snapshot) with TTL. If the snapshot expires, default to safest path (local on-prem or a dedicated fallback pool).

Identity and certificate management:
- Use SPIFFE IDs for workloads. Per-region SPIRE servers mint short-lived certs (5-15 min ttl) with automatic rotation.
- Global coordinator acts as an authority-of-authorities enabling revocation propagation.
- Revocation/compromise procedure: blacklist SPIFFE IDs via global coordinator; region CPs check blacklist on push and enforce immediate connection termination for affected sessions.

Operational considerations and telemetry:
- Trace propagation: library inserts B3/OTel headers; region CP ensures sample continuity during cross-region handoffs by tagging traces with routing decisions.
- Per-route metrics emitted at request egress point: selected-path-id, score-component breakdown (latency, cost, availability), decision timestamp, control-plane-version.
- SLOs to track: egress decision latency (target <10ms), TLS handshake overhead (target <5ms median with optimized path), cross-region failover time (target <200ms for established connections, <500ms for new requests).

Compatibility matrix:
- Proxyless mode supported on: Linux kernel X.y or later with TLS offload, container runtimes that allow CAP_NET_RAW-like hooks, and our supported language runtimes (Go/Java/Python).
- Sidecar mode: all runtimes. Sidecar required for platforms that cannot run the library (Windows-based infra, air-gapped with restricted kernel changes).

Security tradeoffs and mitigations:
- Risk: removing a sidecar reduces an L7 policy enforcement point. Mitigation: surface the same policy checks into the proxyless library and enforce at egress (deny lists, rate limiting, mTLS verification).
- Risk: kernel/TLS offload differences across cloud vendors. Mitigation: maintain a tested compatibility matrix and an eBPF-based observability shim for platforms with inconsistent stacks.

Migration plan (phased):
- Phase 0 (experiment): prototype library + region CP in dev region; smoke tests for latency and correctness. PR: github.com/.../pull/78 (prototype).
- Phase 1 (canary): enable proxyless for a small set of non-critical services (PLAT-4123). Monitor TLS overhead and route decisions.
- Phase 2 (scale): on-board latency-sensitive inference services with strict measurement windows. Provide sidecar fallback toggle for each service.
- Phase 3 (optimize): expand to batch workloads and tune scoring weights.

Testing checklist (what to run):
- Chaos: regional CP partition while traffic flows — ensure fallback uses cached signed snapshot and connections degrade per policy.
- Cert rotation: induce rapid rotation and confirm no request failure during rolling changes.
- Performance: compare tail latency with sidecar vs proxyless for a p99-critical workload.
- Security: run simulated SPIFFE compromise and validate revocation propagation within expected windows.

Open questions / trade-offs to resolve:
- How short should cert TTLs be before rotation cost harms throughput? (5 min vs 15 min trade-off)
- Global coordinator failure modes: do we need active-active global coordinators or a single leader with hot-standby?
- Observability overhead: is additional telemetry in the proxyless library acceptable at scale?
- Cost model: how to incorporate fine-grained per-token hardware cost into real-time scoring without excessive telemetry churn?

Action items / TODOs:
- [Asha] draft a minimal library API (socket wrapper + identity fetch + trace hooks) — due 2024-12-12.
- [Miguel] run a benchmark comparing p99 with sidecar vs proxyless on a 8-GPU inference node — due 2024-12-20.
- [Jinsoo] sketch the global coordinator replication format and signing model — due 2024-12-08.
- Platform-arch sync: add this topic to next Tuesday sync and solicit SRE feedback.

Notes / informal thoughts:
- This pattern tries to balance runtime efficiency and the control we need for tenant-specific policies. It may reduce CPU pressure on nodes when sidecars are expensive, but will require rigorous compatibility testing across clouds and careful cert management.
- If proxyless proves brittle on older kernels, we should keep sidecar as a first-class supported path and make the library optional via feature flags.

References and earlier work:
- Confluence draft: https://confluence.redwood/PLAT/proxyless-egress-draft
- Prototype PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/routing-prototypes/pull/78
- Jira: PLAT-4123 (proxyless canary), PLAT-4170 (egress scoring engine)
- Slack discussion: #platform-arch thread on 2024-11-14

End of note.
